_note: Coding record for the census of completeness denominators, session 156, 2026-09-09. Every code carries the passage it was made from, the URL, the route by which the passage was obtained and the date. Nothing here is coded from training memory: a source that could not be fetched is coded U and says why. Scheme fixed in PREREGISTRATION.md before any source was opened.

axis_a.S: schema-fixed denominator: the count of possible cells is fixed by a schema, profile or field list, independent of what a given record carries
axis_a.P: present-key denominator: only fields actually present on a record contribute to that record's denominator
axis_a.N: third basis, named under kill condition K4: counts reported with no denominator and no ratio at all
axis_a.U: undetermined from what could be reached

sources.reading: Gives Q_comp = sum(P(i))/N with P(i)=1 where the i-th field has a non-null value, and N the number of fields defined in the metadata standard; then a weighted form Q_wcomp = sum(a_i*P(i))/sum(a_i). The denominator is the standard's field list, not the record's. The text attributes the computations to Ochoa & Duval, reference [20].

quotes: Traditional metrics provide a general overview of the makeup of metadata records in a collection, such as the percentage of records with data values for a particular metadata element, which outlines overall usage in the collection.

quotes: Completeness refers to the degree to which all required information is present in a particular dataset.
The degree to which subject data associated with an entity has values for all expected attributes and related entity instances in a specific context of use.
sources.reading: A vocabulary, not a metric: it defines completeness as a dimension and specifies no computation, so no denominator can be read off it. Both wordings point outside the record — 'all required information', 'all expected attributes' — but neither fixes a denominator. Coded U, and see the K4 note: our scheme had no code for a source that defines completeness without measuring it, so U here means something different from U elsewhere in this table.
